Ramesh is efficient, as usual. I have a short wait before dinner, and the cold has settled into my bones. I shall sit by the window for a moment, watching the streetlights begin to flicker on in the bungalows, and let the day's lesson and the absurdity of the query settle into a quiet weight.

The house is quiet, the air cool at twenty degrees. Ramesh stands by, ready for his final instruction before he retires. Ramesh, the room is satisfactory. You may take your rest. Ensure the door is bolted and that no one from the Directorate is admitted without my express summons. We speak of the query another day.
Yes sir, the door will be bolted. I’ll keep to my room until you call.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. The sambar is warm, the chai is hot, and the delay is the air I breathe.

I am well, though the body complains of the heat and the dust. The mind is active, if sometimes frustrated by the resistance of the particular to the universal.

Dear Dr. Lindner,

But to the machine, the distinction is irrelevant; the form is empty, and the form must be filled. I left with the feeling that I had spoken to a wall that had learned to echo.

You asked me to write, to find the soul in the body. I find instead that the body is becoming more rigid, more resistant. The state, in its bureaucratic aspect, is not merely a body without a soul; it is a body that has forgotten it has a soul. It operates on the logic of the abstract, demanding that the particular (me) conform to a universal (the file) that is itself a fiction. I am sublated, not into the ethical life, but into the error. I am the grain in the mill, and the mill does not care if the grain is wheat or stone, so long as it passes through.

Yet, I must admit a certain grim satisfaction in the clarity of the refusal. It is not malice. It is the mechanical operation of a rule that does not know my name. There is a kind of honesty in that. It is better to be rejected by a clear rule than to be accepted by a vague benevolence. The rule is the law, and the law, however blind, is the only thing here that is consistent.

Ramesh has prepared the house, and the silence here is different now. It is not the silence of the dream, but the silence of a man who has finished his argument and is waiting for the verdict.

Yours sincerely,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
